title: Tokenization
subtitle: How text becomes tokens, BPE, and counting tokens
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: LLMs don't work with raw characters or whole words. They need a consistent, compact, vocabulary-limited representation. Character-based models have too many steps; word-based models struggle with rare words and typos.
whyItExists.solution: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds a vocabulary of ~100K sub-word units. Common words become single tokens; rare words split into sub-word parts. This handles any input gracefully.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Token counting matters everywhere: cost estimation, context budget management, chunking documents for RAG, and knowing why some languages are cheaper/more expensive than English.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: You don't need to manually tokenize unless you're building a tokenization library or training your own model. Use provider APIs and tiktoken for counting.

explainModes.beginner: Think of tokens as puzzle pieces that make up text. 'Hello' might be one piece, but 'tokenization' might be three pieces: 'token', 'iz', 'ation'. LLMs only understand these pieces, not letters or full words.
explainModes.simple: LLMs convert text into numbers (tokens) using a lookup table of about 100,000 common text chunks. 'Hello world' might be 2 tokens; a rare technical word might be 5. This affects both cost and what the model can process at once.
explainModes.standard: Tokenizers use Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to build a vocabulary by iteratively merging the most frequent character pairs. The result is sub-word tokens: common words are single tokens, rare words split into multiple. Models process token IDs, not text.
explainModes.technical: GPT-4 uses cl100k_base tokenizer (100K vocab). Claude uses its own tokenizer. BPE merges: start with individual bytes, iteratively merge the most frequent pair until vocabulary size is reached. Sentence boundaries are not respected — tokens can span spaces ('Ġhello' in some tokenizers).
explainModes.deepDive: Unicode handling matters: a CJK character (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) is typically 1-2 tokens, while an ASCII word is 1 token. Emojis are 1-3 tokens. Code is token-heavy because identifiers and operators appear less frequently in training data than prose. tiktoken uses regex pre-tokenization to split on whitespace/punctuation before BPE.

content.text: LLMs do not operate on characters or words. They use sub-word tokenization (Byte-Pair Encoding, or BPE) which breaks text into variable-length chunks from a fixed vocabulary. English averages ~0.75 words per token, so 1000 words ≈ 1333 tokens. API pricing is charged per token.

content.definition: A tokenization algorithm that builds a vocabulary by iteratively merging the most frequent character pairs. 'tokenization' → ['token', 'ization'] or ['token', 'iz', 'ation'] depending on the vocabulary.
The fixed set of all possible tokens a model knows. GPT-4 uses ~100,257 tokens. Each token is an integer ID; the model never sees raw text — only these integers.

content.code:
import tiktoken  # pip install tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4")  # cl100k_base

# Count tokens for a string
text = "Hello, world!"
tokens = enc.encode(text)
print(f"Tokens: {tokens}")       # [9906, 11, 1917, 0]
print(f"Count:  {len(tokens)}")  # 4

# See the actual text pieces
for token_id in tokens:
    print(f"  {token_id:6d} -> '{enc.decode([token_id])}'")

# Token-heavy example: code vs prose
code = 'def fibonacci(n): return n if n <= 1 else fibonacci(n-1) + fibonacci(n-2)'
print(f"\nCode: {len(enc.encode(code))} tokens for {len(code)} chars")
prose = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river"
print(f"Prose: {len(enc.encode(prose))} tokens for {len(prose)} chars")

content.text: Counting Tokens via the Anthropic API

content.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# Count tokens BEFORE making a full API call (saves money on large prompts)
count_response = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-opus-4-5",
    system="You are a helpful assistant that answers concisely.",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Explain the difference between TCP and UDP in simple terms."}
    ]
)
print(f"Input tokens: {count_response.input_tokens}")  # e.g., 35

# After a real call, usage is included in the response
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-5-5",
    max_tokens=200,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"}]
)
print(f"In: {response.usage.input_tokens}, Out: {response.usage.output_tokens}")

content.text: Token Counts by Language and Content Type

items: Python/JS code: ~1 token per 3-4 characters (more expensive)
Chinese/Japanese: 1-2 chars per token (more expensive than English)
Numbers: each digit is often its own token (123 = 3 tokens)
Whitespace and newlines: each takes tokens — compact prompts cost less

content.text: Code uses more tokens per character than English. A Python function of 100 characters may use 50-80 tokens. When building RAG systems, account for this when setting chunk sizes.
Tokenizers differ between providers: Claude, GPT-4, and Llama use different tokenizers. Never assume token counts transfer between providers. Always use the provider's own tokenizer or counting API.

content.code:
import tiktoken

def estimate_cost_gpt4(text: str, is_input: bool = True) -> float:
    """Rough cost estimate for GPT-4o at Nov 2026 pricing."""
    enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4")
    n_tokens = len(enc.encode(text))
    # GPT-4o: $5/1M input tokens, $15/1M output tokens
    price_per_million = 5.0 if is_input else 15.0
    cost = (n_tokens / 1_000_000) * price_per_million
    return cost, n_tokens

system_prompt = "You are a JSON-only API. Respond with valid JSON."
user_msg = "Extract the name and email from: John Smith <john@acme.com>"

cost, tokens = estimate_cost_gpt4(system_prompt + user_msg)
print(f"Input: {tokens} tokens, estimated cost: ${cost:.5f}")

questions.question: Why does tokenization matter for LLM API costs?
options: LLMs charge per second of compute time
API pricing is based on input and output token count
More tokens make models less accurate
questions.explanation: LLM API pricing is based on tokens in and out. Understanding tokenization helps estimate and control costs — especially important at scale.

questions.question: Which type of content uses the MOST tokens per character?
questions.explanation: Code is token-heavy because programming syntax (operators, punctuation, identifiers) appears less frequently in training data than prose, so they don't merge into large tokens.

questions.question: What algorithm do most modern LLM tokenizers use?
questions.explanation: BPE builds a vocabulary by iteratively merging the most frequent character pairs, resulting in sub-word tokens that handle rare words gracefully.

faq.a: Yes. Claude, GPT-4, and Llama use different tokenizers. Never assume token counts transfer between providers. Always use the provider's own counting API (e.g., Anthropic's count_tokens endpoint).

faq.q: How do I estimate the cost of a large batch job?
faq.a: Use tiktoken to count tokens for a sample of your data, multiply by your dataset size, then multiply by the model's per-token price. The count_tokens API endpoint also works without incurring generation costs.

faq.q: What is the max tokens parameter for?
faq.a: max_tokens sets the maximum number of tokens the model is ALLOWED to generate in its response. It does not control input length. Setting it too low truncates responses mid-sentence.
